question: What caused the Great Fire of Hensbrook in 1922?
passage: Hensbrook likes to market itself as 'the town that rebuilt itself,' a slogan that conveniently glosses over the fact that it only needed rebuilding because half of it burned down in 1922. The historical society's plaque outside the courthouse commemorates the event with admirable vagueness, noting only that 'a fire of considerable size consumed forty-one buildings along Market Street before volunteer crews from three neighboring townships managed to contain it near the old grain exchange.' Contemporary newspaper accounts, at least the fragments that survived in the county archive, spend most of their column space praising the bravery of the bucket brigades and listing which prominent families lost their homes, rather than offering any explanation for how the blaze actually started. A popular local theory blames a spark from the blacksmith's forge on Elm Street, though the blacksmith himself apparently testified under oath that his forge had been cold for two days prior. Another theory, favored mostly by people who enjoy a good conspiracy, points to a rival town's grudge over a disputed rail contract, though no evidence beyond gossip has ever surfaced. The rebuilding effort that followed is far better documented: the town adopted its first brick-construction ordinance within the year, established a paid fire department in 1924, and built the water tower that still stands on Cobble Hill today. Whatever actually started the fire, Hensbrook seems to have decided the story of the recovery was more flattering to tell than the story of the cause.
